transcript.position: Singapore asks for a settlement that stops a repeat of 2015, when the 24-hour PSI passed 300 and regional losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars. That outcome needs attribution that outlasts this episode, so we ask Indonesia to release full concession maps to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System, because without maps no one can show which company's land was burning, and the 2002 ASEAN Agreement has no court to settle the question (Article 27). We also ask for a joint ASEAN panel to review corporate attribution cases, and for a full peatland moratorium with no exemptions, because existing concessions are where the fires start. In return, Singapore will help fund the transition through a partial donor fund, but only with measurable reductions in fire and haze days as the condition for each tranche, because we cannot pay for a transition that shows no result. The most damaging objection is sovereignty, so we answer it directly: the maps go to a regional ASEAN body and not to Singapore alone, and the enforcement forum is joint and not Singapore's own courts, which is a real concession from the Act's reach over conduct abroad (section 4). Singapore's Act caps total fines at S$2 million (section 5(5)), so the penalty is small next to the damage and aims at corporate accountability, not at the Indonesian state. If Indonesia accepts the maps and the panel, we can discuss how the moratorium is phased and how the funding is paced.

key_claims.claim: Attribution needs concession maps, and the regional treaty has no court to supply the missing evidence.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 27 says disputes are settled by consultation or negotiation with no tribunal, and [S2] section 8 presumes the land owner caused the haze, with ownership provable from maps supplied by a foreign government, so shared maps are the only way to apply either route without a standoff.

key_claims.claim: The harm in 2015 was large enough that sovereignty cannot be the only consideration.
key_claims.evidence: [Background] Between June and October 2015 the 24-hour PSI passed 300, schools closed and regional economic losses ran into the tens of billions of dollars, while [S1] Article 3(1) pairs the sovereign right to use resources with a duty not to damage other states.

key_claims.claim: Singapore's legal pressure on companies is modest and proportionate, so a joint panel is a fair compromise.
key_claims.evidence: [S2] section 5(2)(a) sets fines of up to S$100,000 per day of haze, but section 5(5) caps the total at S$2 million, and Singapore is offering a joint ASEAN panel instead of applying its Act directly.

key_claims.claim: Funding will be tied to results, which protects donors and gives Indonesia a clear path to money.
key_claims.evidence: [S1] Article 9 already obliges parties to control open burning and prevent land clearing by fire, so tranche payments linked to measured reductions only enforce an existing duty; the 2016 Peatland Restoration Agency under [Background] Presidential Regulation 1/2016 is the natural recipient.

concessions: Singapore will not insist on applying its own Act directly and will accept a joint ASEAN panel, if the maps are released in full to the ASEAN Haze Monitoring System.
Singapore will contribute to a partial donor fund for the transition, but only if disbursement depends on measured reductions in fires and haze.
red_lines: No settlement without a working attribution mechanism, because without it the next dry season repeats 2015 with no way to identify who is responsible.
No transition funding without measurable reductions, because unconditional money would not stop hazardous PSI days and would not be defensible to donors or Singapore's voters.

transcript.position: Indonesia proposes that enforcement against anyone who burns on Indonesian soil stays with Indonesian courts and the Indonesian government, that parcel-level concession maps stay under Indonesian data law, and that the cost of the peatland moratorium be carried by a fully funded donor facility. The 2015 haze, with Singapore's PSI above 300 and regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars [Background], is a real harm, and we accept that fires must stop. However, the ASEAN Agreement already balances this: Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right to use its own resources while barring damage to neighbours, and Article 27 settles disputes by consultation because no court or tribunal exists [S1]. Singapore's Act reaches conduct abroad (section 4), presumes liability from land ownership (section 8) and lets private claimants sue (section 6) [S2], so applying it would put a foreign court in judgment over acts on our soil. That is a red line for us, and it would also hand a foreign claimant a tool over land whose tenure is still disputed, which would produce wrongful attributions.\n\nBecause we want the fires to stop, we offer something real in return. Indonesia will accept a full moratorium on peatland clearing with no exemptions, to be run by the Peatland Restoration Agency, on one condition: a fully funded donor facility must pay for alternatives for smallholders, because we cannot impose a ban on farmers who are about to plant without a funded livelihood alternative. The most damaging objection is that without maps no one can tell who burned. We answer that Article 8(1) already obliges us to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals [S1], so hotspot data will flow, while attribution and prosecution remain with Indonesian courts. El Nino conditions with a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter [ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, 13 August 2015] make a funded, enforceable moratorium urgent, which is why we ask donors to commit now. If partners want more on maps, we can discuss district-level aggregation, but only in exchange for movement on funding and on enforcement.

key_claims.claim: A foreign statute applied to acts on Indonesian soil would create the foreign jurisdiction that Indonesia cannot accept, and the ASEAN framework already provides a consultative route instead.
key_claims.evidence: Article 27 of the ASEAN Agreement settles disputes by consultation or negotiation with no court or tribunal, and Article 3(1) keeps each party's sovereign right to use its own resources, so applying the Singapore Act would go beyond what the parties agreed [S1].

key_claims.claim: The Singapore Act's presumption of liability rests on land ownership, which is unreliable where tenure is disputed, so it risks wrongly blaming the wrong parties.
key_claims.evidence: Section 8 presumes the owner or occupier of burning land caused the haze and allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a foreign government, while section 4 extends the Act to conduct outside Singapore [S2].

key_claims.claim: Indonesia already meets its data duty by sending fire and haze data to the regional centre, so withholding parcel-level maps does not blind the region.
key_claims.evidence: Article 8(1) requires each party's monitoring centre to send fire and haze data to the ASEAN Co-ordinating Centre at agreed intervals, and it says nothing about parcel-level concession maps [S1].

key_claims.claim: The 2015 crisis and the coming El Nino make a funded moratorium urgent, and a ban without funded alternatives would hurt smallholders in the planting window.
key_claims.evidence: The 2015 haze took Singapore's PSI above 300 with regional losses in the tens of billions of dollars [Background], and El Nino has a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter [ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, 13 August 2015].

concessions: Conditional on a fully funded donor facility, Indonesia accepts a full peatland moratorium with no exemptions, run by the Peatland Restoration Agency.
Conditional on movement on enforcement and funding, Indonesia could discuss district-level aggregated concession data instead of withholding it.
red_lines: No foreign jurisdiction over acts on Indonesian soil: the Singapore Act cannot be applied to conduct in Indonesia.
No restriction may fall on smallholders without funded alternatives, so any moratorium requires donor funding.

transcript.position:
We have moved on funding: Singapore now accepts that donors fund the transition in full, which is what Indonesia asked for, and we keep our other asks, in exchange for maps going to the regional monitoring system. Indonesia's strongest point is that applying the Singapore Act would put a foreign court in judgment over acts on its soil, and that tenure is disputed, so liability might fall on the wrong party. We answer by giving up the Act in this settlement: enforcement goes to a joint ASEAN panel, not Singapore's courts, and the Act's S$2 million aggregate cap (section 5(5)) shows the penalty is limited [S2]. Disputed tenure is also the reason maps are needed, not a reason to withhold them, because section 8 allows ownership to be proved from maps supplied by a government [S2], and without maps the presumption cannot be tested and wrongful blame becomes more likely. Indonesia says Article 8(1) already covers its data duty, but that article covers fire and haze data, not who holds each parcel [S1]. Hotspots alone show where it burned, not which company is responsible, and Article 27 provides no tribunal to resolve that gap [S1].

In return for Indonesia accepting full maps to the regional monitoring system and a joint panel, Singapore will back the full moratorium run by the Peatland Restoration Agency and will support a fully funded donor facility, which removes Indonesia's stated red line on smallholders. Two safeguards answer the risks neither side addressed. First, funding is released in tranches against measured reductions in fires on concession land, adjusted for El Nino conditions that have a greater than 90% chance of lasting through the 2015-16 northern winter [ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, 13 August 2015], so Indonesia is not penalised for weather it cannot control, while donors still do not pay for a ban that Article 9 already requires [S1]. Second, to deal with commercial-data and civil-suit exposure, the maps would be held by the ASEAN monitoring system for attribution review by the panel and not published, and I would ask that this access rule be written into the agreement. If Indonesia refuses full maps entirely, we cannot accept a settlement with no attribution mechanism, but we can discuss staged release, starting with the worst-burning districts, as long as parcel-level access for the panel follows.

recommendation.plain_summary: Offer to leave enforcement to Indonesian courts and not apply our Act, in return for full concession maps held by the ASEAN monitoring system and company-naming outcome reports. Release donor money only against measured fire reductions, so any haze or attribution gain is paid for by results.

recommender_rubric.justification: Feasibility (4): The opening package matches Indonesia's Round 3 offer on maps, enforcement and funding, so it is close to a deal. Two things hold it back. The "Indonesia and plantation firms should bear restoration costs" rationale contradicts the full donor fund the package asks for. The options also never address donor pledges before the planting window. Tradeoff coverage (4): It covers the main tensions: sovereignty against attribution, funding against results, and smallholder exemptions against moratorium integrity. Each option names its risks, including the section 6 private-suit exposure, unnamed donors, and exemptions used as cover for burning. It omits any concrete shortfall rule and does not say how the moratorium differs from the "full_no_exemptions" Singapore asked for earlier. Priority consistency (4): Both red lines are served. Attribution comes through maps plus outcome reporting, and funding is tied to measured, El Nino-adjusted results. Accepting partial_exemptions while Singapore had pushed for none is a real concession, and the recommendation handles it with the lapse-by-district mechanism. The rationale about firms bearing costs is inconsistent with the package. Counterpart consideration (4): It accommodates Indonesia's red lines on foreign jurisdiction and on smallholders, and it accepts the access-only restriction on maps. The recommendation does not engage Indonesia's request that Singapore help secure written donor pledges, and it treats the section 6 exposure mainly as a risk to Singapore. Strong arguments (4): It uses the best debate points: Article 27 means a panel has no binding power, maps are tested for attribution, the two-dry-season reopening trigger, and the interim fire-watch period. It leaves out the shortfall-triggers-renewed-talks point and the proposal that parcel records be used in Indonesian prosecutions. Options (3 listed, 3 distinct): The options are conditional branches on different issues (maps and enforcement, funding and exemptions, and the district-data fallback), so they are not rewordings of each other.
